source.title: Bringing the Discussion of Minima Sharpness to the Audio Domain: A Filter-Normalised Evaluation for Acoustic Scene Classification
source.authors: Manuel Milling; Andreas Triantafyllopoulos; Iosif Tsangko; S. D. N. Rampp; Björn Schuller

record.tranche_reason: Tests the sharpness–generalization relationship in acoustic scene classification, an audio setting, using filter-normalized sharpness and reporting results for in-domain and out-of-domain data.
record.gate_note: The paper reports correlations between sharpness and test accuracy for its trained model states, which bear directly on V7. It also states that optimizer choice affects sharpness more than test accuracy; Figure 4 gives the grouped values only visually.
record.test_reason: Tests the sharpness–generalization relationship in acoustic scene classification using weight-magnitude-scaled filter perturbations. This extends V7 to audio with a different sharpness estimator.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: sharper minima tended to generalize better in these exploratory audio experiments, especially on unseen devices. Optimizer-dependent sharpness, uncertain convergence, and sensitivity to sampled directions limit interpretation and practical use.
record.recipe_differences: Uses filter-normalized two-dimensional loss-landscape visualizations and a derived sharpness measure on acoustic scene classification models; it does not use the magnitude-aware perturbation comparison specified in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice affects sharpness more than test accuracy. The authors note that learning-rate and optimizer choices were not independent, limiting their separate interpretation.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP), 2023
record.problems: Exploratory analysis; only 38 trained model states. Sharpness robustness was assessed with three random directions, with a few states showing high standard deviations. The authors note that convergence status and individual hyperparameter effects need further analysis; learning rates and optimizers were not independent. Training accuracy was nearly 100%, rather than stated as exactly 100%.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
The stated image and language benchmarks and a controlled comparison under limited versus broader optimizer tuning.
Batches beyond a workload-dependent threshold and remedies involving training duration or recipe changes.

The original magnitude-aware training-error tolerance estimator; comparisons against norm and margin measures; CIFAR-10 and SVHN without augmentation; verified similarly low training loss and convergence.
Removing highly memorized examples versus matched random removals.

missing.what: Figure 4 also compares average test accuracy across optimizers and batches 16 versus 32 under the same 50-epoch budget. These comparisons are omitted from the rows; their directions and values cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied figure text.
missing.versions: V4, V5: potential audio-setting extensions; cannot assign verdicts from the supplied rendering.

record.verdict_notes: R1 and R2 pool 38 model states; they do not establish the relationship within each architecture or optimizer. The result qualifies extension of V7 rather than directly overturning its specific image-domain finding. Optimizer and learning-rate choices were not independent.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization compared with natural-label generalization was not tested.
Network width and test error across the interpolation threshold were not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures were not compared.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD were not evaluated for the version’s held-out performance claim.
Batch size and its effect on held-out performance were not evaluated as the claim describes.

The study uses filter-normalized two-dimensional visualizations and a derived sharpness measure, not the magnitude-aware perturbation comparison in the version. It tests acoustic scene classification rather than CIFAR-10 or SVHN, and does not compare against norm- or margin-based measures or test the cited sharpness-alone failure cases.
Memorized examples were not identified, removed, or compared with random removals.

relationships.condition: Extension to DCASE2020 audio CNNs using filter-normalized two-dimensional loss sharpness, pooled across architectures and training configurations.
relationships.reason: R1 and R2 report positive sharpness–accuracy correlations (.49 OOD; .28 ID), reversing the expected direction in this extension; the different estimator and domain limit extrapolation to V7's original setting.
relationships.display_finding: Two-dimensional loss sharpness correlated positively with accuracy (0.49 out of distribution; 0.28 in distribution), without establishing the specified training-error tolerance relationship.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Extension to DCASE2020 audio CNNs using filter-normalized two-dimensional loss sharpness, pooled across architectures and training configurations.
labels.reason: R1 and R2 establish a reversed association for a different sharpness estimator and pooled audio models. They do not establish failure or incompleteness of V7's specified tolerance measure under its stated conditions; untested components cannot justify limits_scope.

relation.reason: Its experiments address the broader sharpness–generalization discussion, but do not operationalize V7's specified perturbation-tolerance effect.

tranche.reason: Relative to the supplied claim versions, this study evaluates a related construct: fixed-radius, filter-normalized loss sharpness. It does not measure V7's tolerance before training error rises or compare its gap ranking with norm- and margin-based measures. A new audio setting alone does not establish a test of the specified version.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased for their exploratory estimator. Nearly perfect training accuracy is explicitly reported; similarly low training loss and convergence remain unverified, and optimizer–learning-rate confounding limits interpretation.

statements.correction: OOD sharpness–accuracy correlation=.49; ID correlation=.28; all discussed states have nearly 100% training accuracy; one minus test accuracy approximates the generalization gap; similarly low training loss and convergence are not established; V7 perturbation-tolerance estimator and comparative ranking are untested.
statements.problem: The correlations and conditions are correct, but limits_scope is not justified for the specified V7 measure. The outcome distinction also needs qualification: the authors explicitly interpret one minus test accuracy as the generalization gap because training accuracy is nearly perfect.

statements.correction: Section 3.4 reports nearly 100% training accuracy for all discussed states and interprets one minus test accuracy as the generalization gap; the sharpness estimator measures loss increases at a fixed perturbation radius, not tolerance before training error rises.
statements.problem: The estimator distinction is correct, but saying the result does not concern a training–test gap overlooks the paper's explicit gap interpretation.
